title: Flux-tunable global and local superconductivity in a topological insulator nano-SQUID
authors: Ella Nikodem, Jakob Schluck, Michał Papaj, Max Geier, Mahasweta Bagchi, Liang Fu, Henry F. Legg, Yoichi Ando
abstract: Topological systems are defined by global properties that enforce the existence of local boundary modes. Three-dimensional topological insulators (TIs) were among the earliest proposed systems for hosting topological superconductivity, but experimental focus subsequently shifted to other platforms. Here, we revisit bulk-insulating TIs using a columnar nano-superconducting quantum interference device (nano-SQUID) architecture. This geometry optimises the proximity effect on the TI surface and enables simultaneous probing of global superconducting properties - via the critical current through the nano-SQUID - alongside the local states at the ends of the nano-SQUID via tunnel junctions. We observe several global superconducting features that appear to show a flux-driven global phase transition consistent with entering the topological regime, including periodic critical current oscillations and a sign reversal in the superconducting diode effect. Simultaneously, tunnelling spectroscopy reveals spectral jumps in local and nonlocal conductance that align with these global features. However, zero-bias peaks (ZBPs) in local conductance are present both within the predicted topological range of magnetic fields and in theoretically trivial regimes, including at zero magnetic field. Ultimately, the lack of correlation between local ZBP signatures and global signatures emphasises that conclusively identifying Majorana bound states will necessitate a combined approach, integrating the establishment of global topological properties with the use of local and other, more advanced, probes.
summary: This paper investigates topological superconductivity in a TI nano-SQUID by measuring both global critical currents and local tunneling conductance. While global measurements show clear, flux-tunable signatures consistent with a topological phase transition, the local measurements yield ambiguous results. The authors conclude that a combined, integrated approach is necessary to definitively confirm the presence of Majorana bound states.
main_problem: The study aims to investigate and conclusively identify topological superconductivity, motivated by the search for Majorana bound states (MBSs), in a solid-state platform.
main_result: Global superconducting signatures (e.g., $h/2e$ flux periodicity and SDE reversal) are observed, suggesting a topological phase transition, but local measurements show ambiguous zero-bias peaks that do not correlate robustly with global signatures.
method: The research combines global transport measurements (critical current, superconducting diode effect) with local tunneling spectroscopy and nonlocal conductance measurements on a nano-SQUID structure.
model_or_system: The physical system is a three-dimensional topological insulator (TI) nanowire proximitized by a superconductor, configured as a nano-SQUID. The system's superconducting properties are tuned by an external axial magnetic flux ($\Phi$) and gate voltage ($V_b$).
key_observables: Critical current ($I_c$), superconducting diode effect (SDE) polarity, zero-bias conductance peaks (ZBPs), and nonlocal conductance ($G_{LL}, G_{RL}$).
important_parameters: Axial magnetic flux ($\Phi$), gate voltage ($V_G$), and the superconducting flux quantum ($\Phi_0 = h/2e$).
main_assumptions: The authors caution that the lack of correlation between local ZBP signatures and global signatures implies that conclusively identifying MBSs requires integrating global topological property establishment with advanced local probes.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the device structure, $I_c$ vs. $B_x$ showing oscillations, and simultaneous measurements comparing global $I_c$ anomalies with local conductance spectral jumps and nonlocal conductance changes across different flux regimes.
paper_structure: The paper systematically presents global measurements demonstrating flux-tunable topological signatures, followed by local spectroscopy confirming spectral jumps, and concludes by analyzing the correlation (or lack thereof) between these local and global findings to address the ambiguity of MBS identification.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses the experimental challenge of verifying topological superconductivity by comparing macroscopic (global) transport signatures with microscopic (local) spectroscopic signatures, which is highly relevant to open quantum systems research.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Flux-tunable transport and local spectroscopy in a nano-SQUID. a, Scanning electron microscope (SEM) image of the device. An exfoliated topological-insulator (TI) flake is patterned into a nanowire (pink) by dry etching. The etched regions are filled with Nb (green), forming a sandwich junction. Residual TI fragments do not participate in transport. Gold electrodes contact the TI nanowire via tunnel junctions TJ1 and TJ2, enabling local probing of the density of states. b, Schematic of the baseline device, featuring the TI nanowire core, the superconducting shell, tunnel dielectric, and a single functional TJ. c, Energy-phase dispersion of the perpendicular (kx = 0) mode in a TI...

FIG. 2. Theory of topological superconductivity in a TI nano- SQUID. a, Calculated ground-state phase difference, explicitly map- ping the 0 −π transition to topological boundaries. b, Calculated Ic and η vs. flux Φ. c, Simulated energy spectrum as a function of Φ, showing the spectral jumps at the values of the topological phase transition and the emergence of zero-energy modes in regions with an odd number of flux quanta.

FIG. 3. Simultaneous global and dual-local spectroscopy. a, Global Ic and η in device B. Note that the cross-section is larger than for device A and multiple oscillations of Ic are observed. b, c, Dif- ferential conductance measured simultaneously at TJ1 (GLL, b) and TJ2 (GRR, c). Abrupt spectral jumps occur at fields commensurate with Ic anomalies. However, there are zero-bias peaks visible in both theoretically topological regimes and trivial regimes. d, e, Nonlocal conductance GLR and GRL showing that some features correspond to the boundaries of the expected topological regimes.

FIG. 4. Gate-voltage dependence and end-to-end correlations. a, b, d, e, g, h GLL and GRR in device B as a function of VG for trivial and topological flux regimes. c, f, i End-to-end correlation analysis using the product of the the third derivative at zero bias. j VG-dependence of Ic (black) and the normal state resistance RN (grey). k VG-dependence of GLL and GRR. l Relative fraction of gate voltages exhibiting correlated zero-bias conductance peaks (red), correlated zero-bias conductance dips (blue), or no correlation (grey) as a function of Bx.
